subtype: Approach: leaving it and returning after a rest [Revision]
passage:
"It's impossible!" Tarun glared at the triangle in his notebook. "Twenty minutes and it still doesn't work!"
"Then close the book," said his mother Neelam. "Go and play."
"But it's homework."
"It will be here when you come back."
Tarun kicked the ball around the courtyard for half an hour. When he came in, red-faced and thirsty, he picked up his pencil and looked at the figure again.
"Oh!" he said. "I wrote AB where it should be BC. I mislabelled the sides!"
He fixed them and finished the problem in five minutes.
"Ma, it was that easy."

qa.q: How long did Tarun stare at the triangle before he stopped?
qa.a: He had worked on it for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he said "It's impossible!"?
qa.a: He was frustrated and stuck. He glared at the notebook and thought twenty minutes should have been enough.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Tarun use the next time he is stuck, and why?
qa.a: He could check the labels on his figure and read the question again before quitting. Small slips in labelling can hide behind a problem that seems impossible.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Tarun's stuck problem?
qa.a: Neelam sees a boy who is tired and wound up, so she sends him to play, trusting the problem will look different afterwards. 😊

grounding: A boy stares at a geometry problem for twenty minutes, goes to play, and on returning sees he mislabelled the sides and finishes it in five.
